title: Traditional founding of Rome by Romulus
summary: According to Roman tradition, Romulus founded the city of Rome on the Palatine Hill on this day. The date was later fixed by the scholar Varro and celebrated each year as the Parilia.
reason: Roman legend tells of the twins Romulus and Remus, who quarrelled over where to found a new city, after which Romulus founded it and gave it his name.
significance: The date became the starting point of the Roman count of years and the birthday of a city that would shape Western civilization.

title: Babylon falls to Cyrus the Great
summary: Persian forces under Cyrus the Great took Babylon, ending the Neo-Babylonian Empire. The city was captured without a major battle after the Babylonian defeat at Opis.
reason: Cyrus was expanding the Achaemenid Empire, and King Nabonidus had lost support among the Babylonian priesthood and population.
significance: It made Persia the dominant power of the Near East and led to the return of exiled Jews to Judah.

title: Philip II of Macedon wins at Chaeronea
summary: Philip II of Macedon and his son Alexander defeated an alliance led by Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea in Boeotia.
reason: Macedon was expanding south, and Athens, urged on by Demosthenes, joined Thebes to stop Philip.
significance: The victory ended the independence of the Greek city states and gave Macedon control of Greece.

title: Alexander defeats Darius III at Issus
summary: Alexander the Great defeated the much larger Persian army of Darius III near Issus in southern Anatolia. Darius fled the field and left his family behind.
reason: Alexander had invaded the Persian Empire, and Darius came in person to stop his advance along the coast.
significance: The victory opened the Levant and Egypt to Alexander and shook Persian authority.

title: Battle of Gaugamela
summary: Alexander the Great decisively defeated Darius III at Gaugamela, east of the Tigris. Darius fled again and was later killed by his own officers.
reason: After losing the western provinces, Darius raised a vast army in Mesopotamia to stop Alexander's march into the Persian heartland.
significance: It brought down the Achaemenid Empire and opened the way for the Hellenistic world.

title: Hannibal ambushes the Romans at Lake Trasimene
summary: Hannibal trapped a Roman army under the consul Gaius Flaminius on the northern shore of Lake Trasimene and destroyed it. Flaminius was killed.
reason: During the Second Punic War Hannibal had crossed the Alps and was seeking to break Roman power in Italy.
significance: It remains one of the largest ambushes in military history and spread panic in Rome.

title: Ptolemy IV defeats Antiochus III at Raphia
summary: The Ptolemaic king Ptolemy IV defeated the Seleucid king Antiochus III near Raphia in southern Palestine, one of the largest battles of the Hellenistic age with war elephants on both sides.
reason: The two Hellenistic kingdoms were fighting the Fourth Syrian War over control of Coele Syria.
significance: It kept Coele Syria under Ptolemaic rule for a time and was the first time Egypt armed large numbers of native Egyptians as phalanx soldiers.

title: Battle of Cannae
summary: Hannibal encircled and destroyed a much larger Roman army at Cannae in Apulia. Tens of thousands of Romans died in a single day.
reason: Rome sought a decisive battle to end Hannibal's campaign in Italy and sent an exceptionally large army against him.
significance: Its double envelopment became a classic of military tactics, studied for more than two thousand years.

title: Scipio defeats Hannibal at Zama
summary: Scipio Africanus defeated Hannibal near Zama in North Africa, ending the Second Punic War in Rome's favour.
reason: Scipio had carried the war to Africa, forcing Carthage to recall Hannibal from Italy to defend the city.
significance: Carthage lost its empire and fleet, and Rome became the leading power of the western Mediterranean.

title: Priests issue the decree later carved on the Rosetta Stone
summary: A council of Egyptian priests meeting at Memphis issued a decree honouring the young king Ptolemy V. Copies were carved in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek, and one of them survives as the Rosetta Stone.
reason: The decree marked the first anniversary of Ptolemy V's coronation and confirmed the priests' privileges in return for their support of the dynasty.
significance: The Rosetta Stone copy allowed Champollion to decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs in the nineteenth century.

title: Julius Caesar crosses the Rubicon
summary: Julius Caesar led a legion across the Rubicon river into Italy proper, defying the Senate's order to disband his army. He is said to have declared that the die was cast.
reason: The Senate, led by Caesar's rivals around Pompey, demanded that he give up his command, which would have exposed him to prosecution.
significance: It began the civil war that ended the Roman Republic, and the phrase became a byword for a point of no return.

title: Caesar defeats Pompey at Pharsalus
summary: Julius Caesar defeated the larger army of Pompey and the Senate at Pharsalus in Thessaly. Pompey fled to Egypt.
reason: The civil war between Caesar and the senatorial faction came to a head in Greece after Caesar's setback at Dyrrhachium.
significance: It broke the senatorial cause and left Caesar the master of the Roman world.

title: Pompey the Great is murdered in Egypt
summary: Pompey, fleeing after his defeat at Pharsalus, was stabbed to death as he landed at Pelusium on the orders of the advisers of the young king Ptolemy XIII.
reason: The Egyptian court hoped to win favour with the victorious Caesar and avoid being drawn into the Roman civil war.
significance: His death removed Caesar's greatest rival and drew Caesar into Egyptian politics and his alliance with Cleopatra.

title: Caesar wins the Battle of Thapsus
summary: Julius Caesar defeated the republican forces of Metellus Scipio and their Numidian ally King Juba I at Thapsus in North Africa.
reason: After Pompey's death his supporters had regrouped in the province of Africa to continue the civil war.
significance: The defeat led to the suicide of Cato the Younger and ended organised republican resistance in Africa.

title: The Julian calendar takes effect
summary: The calendar reform ordered by Julius Caesar came into force, giving the Roman year 365 days with a leap day every four years.
reason: The old Roman lunar calendar had drifted badly out of step with the seasons because intercalation was neglected or abused for political ends.
significance: With small changes it remains the basis of the calendar used worldwide today.

title: Julius Caesar is assassinated
summary: A group of senators led by Brutus and Cassius stabbed Julius Caesar to death at a meeting of the Senate in the Curia of Pompey.
reason: The conspirators feared that Caesar, recently named dictator for life, would make himself king and destroy the Republic.
significance: Instead of saving the Republic, the murder set off new civil wars that ended with Augustus as the first emperor.

title: Cicero is killed on the orders of Mark Antony
summary: The orator and statesman Cicero was caught and killed near his villa at Formiae. His head and hands were displayed in the Forum.
reason: Cicero had attacked Mark Antony in his Philippics, and Antony insisted on his name being placed on the proscription lists of the Second Triumvirate.
significance: His death symbolised the end of the free Republic, and his writings shaped Latin prose for centuries.

title: First Battle of Philippi
summary: The armies of Mark Antony and Octavian met the forces of Brutus and Cassius at Philippi in Macedonia. Cassius killed himself after the first engagement, and Brutus was defeated three weeks later.
reason: The Second Triumvirate set out to avenge Caesar and destroy the army of his assassins in the east.
significance: It ended the cause of Caesar's assassins and left the triumvirs in control of the Roman world.

title: Battle of Actium
summary: Octavian's fleet under Agrippa defeated the fleet of Mark Antony and Cleopatra off Actium in western Greece. Antony and Cleopatra escaped to Egypt.
reason: The alliance between Octavian and Antony had collapsed into open war over power in Rome and Antony's ties to Cleopatra's Egypt.
significance: It left Octavian sole ruler and led to the Roman Empire under Augustus.

title: Mark Antony dies as Octavian takes Alexandria
summary: As Octavian's army entered Alexandria, Mark Antony stabbed himself on hearing a false report of Cleopatra's death and died in her arms. Cleopatra killed herself days later.
reason: After Actium, Antony's forces deserted him, and Octavian advanced on Egypt to finish the war.
significance: Egypt became a Roman province, ending the last great Hellenistic kingdom.

title: The Senate gives Octavian the name Augustus
summary: The Roman Senate granted Octavian the title Augustus, days after he formally returned his extraordinary powers to the Senate and people.
reason: Octavian wanted to rule with supreme power while presenting it as a restored Republic, and the Senate honoured him in return.
significance: It is usually taken as the start of the Roman Empire and the Principate.

title: The poet Virgil dies at Brundisium
summary: Virgil, author of the Aeneid, died at Brundisium after falling ill on a journey back from Greece. He had asked for the unfinished epic to be burned, but Augustus had it published.
reason: Virgil had spent his last decade writing the Aeneid, a national epic for Augustan Rome, and fell ill while travelling.
significance: The Aeneid survived and became the central work of Latin literature.

title: Wang Mang is killed as his Xin dynasty falls
summary: Rebel forces broke into Chang'an and killed the emperor Wang Mang in his palace, ending his Xin dynasty.
reason: Wang Mang's radical reforms, floods of the Yellow River and famine provoked massive revolts such as the Red Eyebrows and the Lulin.
significance: His fall led to the restoration of the Han dynasty as the Eastern Han.

title: Emperor Caligula is assassinated
summary: Officers of the Praetorian Guard led by Cassius Chaerea killed the emperor Caligula in a passage of the palace on the Palatine. The guard then proclaimed his uncle Claudius emperor.
reason: Caligula's cruelty, humiliation of senators and officers, and erratic rule had made many enemies at court.
significance: It showed that the Praetorian Guard could make and unmake emperors.

title: The Great Fire of Rome breaks out
summary: A fire broke out near the Circus Maximus and burned for days, destroying large parts of Rome. Nero blamed the Christians and had many of them executed.
reason: The crowded city of timber buildings was highly flammable, and rumours soon claimed that Nero had wanted the fire to clear land for his palace.
significance: It led to the first Roman persecution of Christians and to the rebuilding of Rome, including Nero's Golden House.

title: Emperor Nero takes his own life
summary: Declared a public enemy by the Senate and abandoned by the Praetorian Guard, Nero killed himself at a villa outside Rome.
reason: Revolts by Vindex and Galba in the provinces had broken Nero's hold on power.
significance: His death ended the Julio-Claudian dynasty and began the Year of the Four Emperors.

title: Emperor Domitian is assassinated
summary: Domitian was stabbed to death in his palace by court officials. The Senate named the elderly senator Nerva emperor the same day.
reason: Domitian's autocratic rule and treason trials had made the Senate and his own household fear for their lives.
significance: Nerva's accession began the era of the Five Good Emperors.

title: Earthquake devastates Antioch
summary: A powerful earthquake destroyed much of Antioch, one of the largest cities of the Roman Empire. Emperor Trajan, wintering there during his Parthian war, escaped with minor injuries.
reason: Antioch lies on the active Dead Sea fault system, where strong earthquakes recur.
significance: It was among the deadliest disasters of the Roman period and nearly killed the emperor.

title: Chinese astronomers record supernova SN 185
summary: Astronomers of the Han dynasty recorded a new star near Alpha Centauri that stayed visible for months. It is the earliest recorded supernova.
reason: The Han court kept careful records of celestial events, which were believed to carry omens for the state.
significance: It is the oldest known record of a supernova, now linked to the remnant RCW 86.

title: Emperor Commodus is strangled
summary: Commodus was strangled in his bath by the wrestler Narcissus in a plot organised by his court officials.
reason: The emperor's erratic rule and plan to appear as a gladiator and consul on New Year's Day alarmed his household and the Praetorian prefect.
significance: His death ended the Nerva Antonine dynasty and led to the civil wars of 193.

title: Han dynasty ends as Cao Pi founds Cao Wei
summary: Emperor Xian of Han abdicated in favour of Cao Pi, who declared himself emperor of the new state of Wei. Four centuries of Han rule ended.
reason: Cao Pi's father Cao Cao had controlled the Han court for decades, and the abdication only made his family's power official.
significance: It opened the Three Kingdoms period as Liu Bei and Sun Quan claimed their own thrones.

title: Diocletian is proclaimed Roman emperor
summary: The army acclaimed Diocletian emperor near Nicomedia after the death of Emperor Numerian. He personally killed the prefect Aper, accused of Numerian's murder.
reason: The Roman Empire was deep in the Crisis of the Third Century, with emperors rapidly made and killed by the army.
significance: His reforms, including the Tetrarchy, ended the crisis and reshaped the late Roman state.

title: The Great Persecution of Christians begins
summary: On the feast of the Terminalia, imperial troops destroyed the new church at Nicomedia, and the next day an edict ordered churches and scriptures destroyed across the empire.
reason: Diocletian and his Caesar Galerius saw the growing Christian church as a threat to the unity and traditional religion of the empire.
significance: It was the last and most severe persecution of Christians in the Roman Empire.

title: Constantine is proclaimed emperor at York
summary: After the death of his father, the emperor Constantius Chlorus, the troops at Eboracum acclaimed Constantine as emperor.
reason: The army in Britain preferred Constantine to the successor chosen under the Tetrarchy's rules.
significance: It started the rise of the man who would reunite the empire and adopt Christianity.

title: Galerius issues the Edict of Serdica
summary: The dying emperor Galerius issued an edict ending the persecution of Christians and allowing them to practise their faith.
reason: Years of persecution had failed to destroy Christianity, and Galerius was gravely ill.
significance: It was the first imperial edict to legalise Christianity, two years before the Edict of Milan.

title: Luoyang falls in the Disaster of Yongjia
summary: Forces of the Xiongnu-led Han Zhao state captured Luoyang, the capital of the Jin dynasty, sacked the city and seized Emperor Huai.
reason: The Jin had been weakened by the War of the Eight Princes, and northern peoples took advantage of the chaos.
significance: It led to the loss of northern China and the move of the Jin court to the south.

title: Battle of the Milvian Bridge
summary: Constantine defeated his rival Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge outside Rome. Maxentius drowned in the Tiber.
reason: The two emperors were fighting for control of the western empire. Constantine reported a vision promising victory under a Christian sign.
significance: It made Constantine master of the West and set him on the path to the Christianization of the empire.

title: Constantine defeats Licinius at Chrysopolis
summary: Constantine defeated the eastern emperor Licinius at Chrysopolis, across the Bosporus from Byzantium.
reason: The uneasy partnership of the two emperors had broken down into a final war for sole control of the empire.
significance: It made Constantine sole ruler of the Roman Empire.

title: The First Council of Nicaea opens
summary: Bishops from across the empire met at Nicaea at the call of Emperor Constantine. The council condemned Arianism and adopted the first version of the Nicene Creed.
reason: The dispute over the teachings of Arius about the nature of Christ was dividing the church, and Constantine wanted religious unity.
significance: It was the first ecumenical council and defined core Christian doctrine.

title: Constantinople is dedicated as the new capital
summary: Constantine formally dedicated his rebuilt city on the site of Byzantium as the new capital of the Roman Empire.
reason: Constantine wanted a capital closer to the threatened eastern and Danube frontiers and free of Rome's old pagan elite.
significance: Constantinople remained the capital of the Eastern Roman Empire for over a thousand years.

title: Emperor Julian dies on campaign in Persia
summary: Julian, the last pagan Roman emperor, died of a wound received in a skirmish with Sasanian forces near Samarra during his retreat from Ctesiphon.
reason: Julian had invaded the Sasanian Empire to win glory and secure the east, but failed to take Ctesiphon.
significance: His death ended the last attempt to restore paganism and forced Rome into a humiliating peace with Persia.

title: Great earthquake and tsunami strike from Crete
summary: A massive earthquake near Crete raised parts of the island and sent a tsunami across the eastern Mediterranean, which devastated Alexandria and other coasts.
reason: Movement on a fault of the Hellenic subduction zone released enormous energy.
significance: It is one of the largest earthquakes known in the Mediterranean and was remembered for centuries in Alexandria.

title: Goths defeat the Roman army at Adrianople
summary: Gothic forces under Fritigern destroyed a Roman army near Adrianople. Emperor Valens was killed.
reason: Goths fleeing the Huns had been admitted into the empire but revolted after abuse by Roman officials.
significance: It showed that barbarian armies could defeat Rome's field army and began the Gothic settlement within the empire.

title: Edict of Thessalonica makes Nicene Christianity the state religion
summary: Emperor Theodosius I, with his co-emperors, decreed that all subjects should profess the Nicene Christian faith.
reason: Theodosius wanted to end the long conflict between Nicene and Arian Christians and to unify the empire under one creed.
significance: It made Nicene Christianity the official religion of the Roman Empire.

title: Theodosius wins the Battle of the Frigidus
summary: Emperor Theodosius I defeated the usurper Eugenius and his general Arbogast in the Vipava valley, helped by a violent wind known as the bora.
reason: Eugenius had been raised to the throne in the West by Arbogast and had the support of the pagan senatorial aristocracy.
significance: It was the last time a Roman emperor ruled both halves of the empire and ended the pagan revival.

title: Death of Theodosius I divides the Roman Empire
summary: Theodosius I died in Milan. The empire passed to his sons, Arcadius in the East and Honorius in the West, and was never again united.
reason: Theodosius had arranged for each son to rule one half of the empire.
significance: It marks the permanent division into the Eastern and Western Roman Empires.

title: Vandals, Alans and Suebi cross the Rhine
summary: A large mixed group of Vandals, Alans and Suebi crossed the Rhine into Roman Gaul, traditionally near Mogontiacum.
reason: Pressure from the Huns and the withdrawal of Roman troops to defend Italy left the frontier weakly defended.
significance: It opened Gaul and Hispania to barbarian invasion and hastened the collapse of the Western Empire.

title: The Visigoths sack Rome
summary: Visigoths under Alaric entered and plundered Rome for three days. It was the first time in 800 years the city fell to a foreign enemy.
reason: Alaric's demands for land and payment for his people were refused by Emperor Honorius in Ravenna.
significance: The sack shocked the Roman world and inspired Augustine to write The City of God.

title: Augustine of Hippo dies during the Vandal siege
summary: Augustine, bishop of Hippo and the most influential theologian of the Latin West, died while the Vandals besieged his city.
reason: The Vandals under Genseric had crossed from Spain into North Africa and were conquering the Roman provinces there.
significance: His works, such as the Confessions and The City of God, shaped Western Christianity and philosophy.

title: The Council of Ephesus opens
summary: The third ecumenical council opened at Ephesus and condemned Nestorius, archbishop of Constantinople, affirming Mary as Theotokos, mother of God.
reason: Nestorius and Cyril of Alexandria were locked in a bitter dispute over how the divine and human natures are united in Christ.
significance: It led to the separation of the Church of the East, which spread Christianity across Asia.

title: The Vandals capture Carthage
summary: Genseric's Vandals seized Carthage by surprise, breaking a treaty with Rome, and made it the capital of their kingdom.
reason: The Vandals sought the rich grain lands of Africa Proconsularis, the bread basket of Rome.
significance: Losing Africa's grain and taxes was a heavy blow to the Western Roman Empire.

title: Aetius and the Visigoths stop Attila
summary: A Roman and Visigothic army under Flavius Aetius and King Theodoric I fought Attila's Huns on the Catalaunian Plains in Gaul. Theodoric was killed, but Attila withdrew.
reason: Attila had invaded Gaul, and Romans and Visigoths put aside their rivalry to face the common threat.
significance: It halted the Hunnic advance into western Europe.

title: The Council of Chalcedon opens
summary: The fourth ecumenical council opened at Chalcedon and defined Christ as one person in two natures, divine and human.
reason: Emperor Marcian and Pope Leo I wanted to overturn the Second Council of Ephesus and settle the dispute over the nature of Christ.
significance: Its definition split the churches, leading to the separation of the Oriental Orthodox churches.

title: The Vandals sack Rome
summary: Vandals under Genseric entered Rome and plundered it for two weeks, carrying off treasure and the empress Licinia Eudoxia and her daughters.
reason: The murder of Emperor Valentinian III broke the treaty with Genseric, who used the chaos to attack.
significance: The thorough plunder gave rise to the word vandalism.

title: Odoacer deposes Romulus Augustulus
summary: The Germanic general Odoacer deposed the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna and ruled Italy as king, sending the imperial regalia to Constantinople.
reason: Odoacer's soldiers had been refused land in Italy by Romulus's father Orestes, and they revolted.
significance: It is the traditional date of the fall of the Western Roman Empire.

title: Nika riots break out in Constantinople
summary: Chariot racing factions at the Hippodrome turned on Emperor Justinian I and set much of Constantinople on fire. After several days the revolt was crushed with the massacre of tens of thousands of people in the Hippodrome.
reason: Anger over heavy taxes, harsh officials and the arrest of faction members united the normally rival Blues and Greens against the emperor.
significance: Justinian survived and used the destruction to rebuild the city, including the new Hagia Sophia.

title: Hagia Sophia is consecrated
summary: Emperor Justinian I dedicated the new church of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, built in under six years. Its vast dome made it the largest church in the world for nearly a thousand years.
reason: The earlier church had burned in the Nika riots, and Justinian wanted a monument to his rule and to Christian faith.
significance: It became a model for Byzantine and later Ottoman architecture and a symbol of the city.

title: Li Yuan proclaims the Tang dynasty
summary: Li Yuan declared himself emperor in Chang'an, founding the Tang dynasty as the Sui dynasty collapsed. He is known as Emperor Gaozu of Tang.
reason: Failed wars in Korea, costly public works and revolts had broken Sui rule, and the murder of Emperor Yang left the throne open.
significance: The Tang ruled China for almost three centuries in a golden age of culture, trade and power.

title: Muslims defeat the Quraysh at the Battle of Badr
summary: A small force led by Muhammad defeated a larger army of the Quraysh of Mecca near the wells of Badr. Several leading Meccans were killed.
reason: The Muslims of Medina had moved to intercept a Meccan caravan, and Mecca sent an army to protect it.
significance: The victory strengthened Muhammad's position in Arabia and is remembered in Islam as a sign of divine support.

title: Li Shimin seizes power in the Xuanwu Gate Incident
summary: Prince Li Shimin ambushed and killed his brothers, the crown prince Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji, at the Xuanwu Gate of the palace in Chang'an. Within weeks his father abdicated in his favor.
reason: A bitter rivalry over the succession had grown between Li Shimin, the dynasty's leading general, and the crown prince.
significance: Li Shimin became Emperor Taizong, one of the most admired rulers in Chinese history.

title: Death of the Prophet Muhammad
summary: Muhammad died in Medina after a short illness, having united much of Arabia under Islam. Abu Bakr was chosen as the first caliph.
reason: He fell ill with a fever shortly after his farewell pilgrimage to Mecca.
significance: The question of his succession shaped the caliphate and the later split between Sunni and Shia Islam.

title: Battle of the Yarmouk begins
summary: The armies of the Rashidun Caliphate under Khalid ibn al-Walid met a large Byzantine army by the Yarmouk River. After six days of fighting the Byzantines were routed.
reason: Emperor Heraclius gathered a great army to drive back the Arab conquest of Syria.
significance: The defeat ended Byzantine rule in Syria and opened the Levant to the spread of Islam.
place: Yarmouk River, near the Syria-Jordan border

title: Caliph Uthman is assassinated in Medina
summary: Rebels besieged the house of the third caliph, Uthman ibn Affan, and killed him while he was reading the Quran. Ali ibn Abi Talib then became caliph.
reason: Many provincial Muslims resented Uthman's favoring of his own Umayyad clan and his choice of governors.
significance: His death led to the First Fitna, the first civil war within the Muslim community.

title: Husayn ibn Ali is killed at the Battle of Karbala
summary: A small group led by Husayn ibn Ali, grandson of Muhammad, was surrounded and killed by an Umayyad army at Karbala. The women and children of his family were taken captive.
reason: Husayn refused to accept Yazid I as caliph and was travelling to Kufa, where supporters had invited him to lead them.
significance: His death is mourned every year on Ashura and became central to Shia Islam.

title: Wu Zetian becomes China's only empress regnant
summary: Wu Zetian, who had long ruled through her husband and sons, took the throne in her own name and proclaimed a new Zhou dynasty. She ruled until 705.
reason: After decades of controlling the Tang court, she removed her son Emperor Ruizong and claimed full imperial authority.
significance: She remains the only woman in Chinese history to rule as emperor in her own right.

title: Charles Martel defeats the Umayyads at the Battle of Tours
summary: Frankish forces under Charles Martel defeated an Umayyad army led by Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi between Poitiers and Tours. The Umayyad commander was killed.
reason: After conquering Iberia, Umayyad armies were raiding north into Gaul, and this force was heading for the rich abbey of Tours.
significance: It halted the northward advance of the caliphate into Western Europe and raised the power of the Carolingian family.

title: The Abbasids defeat the Umayyads at the Battle of the Zab
summary: An Abbasid army crushed the forces of the Umayyad caliph Marwan II by the Great Zab River. Marwan fled and was killed later that year.
reason: The Abbasid revolution, launched in Khurasan, drew on wide discontent with Umayyad rule among non-Arab Muslims and Shia supporters.
significance: It ended the Umayyad Caliphate in the east and brought the Abbasids to power for five centuries.

title: An Lushan launches his rebellion against the Tang
summary: The frontier general An Lushan marched south from his base at Fanyang against the Tang court. He soon took Luoyang and Chang'an and proclaimed his own dynasty.
reason: An Lushan commanded huge armies in the northeast and feared the hostility of the chief minister Yang Guozhong.
significance: The eight-year war killed millions and permanently weakened the Tang dynasty.

title: Caliph al-Mansur founds Baghdad
summary: The Abbasid caliph al-Mansur laid the foundations of a new capital, the round city of Baghdad, on the Tigris. It was planned as a circle with the palace and mosque at its centre.
reason: The Abbasids wanted a capital away from Umayyad Syria, near their supporters in Iraq and Persia and on major trade routes.
significance: Baghdad became the largest city of its age and the centre of the Islamic Golden Age.

title: Charlemagne is crowned emperor in Rome
summary: Pope Leo III crowned the Frankish king Charlemagne as emperor of the Romans in St. Peter's Basilica on Christmas Day.
reason: Charlemagne had protected the pope from his enemies in Rome and ruled most of Western Europe, while the throne in Constantinople was held by a woman, Irene.
significance: It revived the idea of a Western empire and led to the Holy Roman Empire.
place: Old St. Peter's Basilica, Rome, Vatican City

title: Death of Caliph Harun al-Rashid
summary: The Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid died at Tus in Khurasan while on campaign against a rebellion. His empire was divided between his sons al-Amin and al-Ma'mun.
reason: He fell ill while marching east to put down a revolt in Khurasan.
significance: His reign was remembered as the height of Abbasid Baghdad, and the split between his sons led to civil war.

title: Oaths of Strasbourg are sworn
summary: Louis the German and Charles the Bald swore an alliance against their brother Lothair, each in the language of the other's army. The texts were recorded in early forms of French and German.
reason: Charlemagne's grandsons were fighting over the division of the Carolingian Empire.
significance: The oaths are the oldest surviving text in a Romance language that became French.

title: The Diamond Sutra, oldest dated printed book, is made
summary: A woodblock printed copy of the Buddhist Diamond Sutra was produced in Tang China, with a note giving this date. It was found in the Mogao Caves at Dunhuang in 1900.
reason: A man named Wang Jie paid for the printing for the merit of his parents, as Buddhists spread scripture through copies.
significance: It is the earliest dated printed book known, evidence of the Chinese invention of printing.

title: Death of Alfred the Great
summary: Alfred, king of Wessex, died in Winchester after a reign spent defending his kingdom against the Vikings. He was succeeded by his son Edward the Elder.
reason: He died after years of ill health.
significance: His defence of Wessex and support for learning laid the ground for a united kingdom of England.

title: Abd al-Rahman III proclaims the Caliphate of Cordoba
summary: The Umayyad emir of al-Andalus, Abd al-Rahman III, declared himself caliph in Cordoba, rejecting the authority of both the Abbasids and the Fatimids.
reason: He had restored order in al-Andalus and wanted to answer the Fatimids, who had claimed the caliphate in North Africa.
significance: Cordoba became one of the richest and most learned cities of Europe.

title: Otto I defeats the Magyars at the Battle of Lechfeld
summary: King Otto I of Germany destroyed a large Hungarian army that was besieging Augsburg, on the plain by the river Lech.
reason: Magyar horsemen had raided Western Europe for decades and invaded Bavaria again in 955.
significance: It ended the Hungarian raids, and the Magyars settled and soon became a Christian kingdom.

title: Zhao Kuangyin founds the Song dynasty
summary: After his troops proclaimed him emperor at Chen Bridge, the general Zhao Kuangyin took the throne from the child ruler of the Later Zhou and founded the Song dynasty.
reason: Northern China had suffered a series of short military regimes, and the army wanted a strong adult ruler.
significance: The Song reunified most of China and presided over a great age of commerce, technology and learning.

title: Otto I is crowned Holy Roman Emperor
summary: Pope John XII crowned the German king Otto I as emperor in Rome.
reason: The pope needed protection against Berengar II of Italy, and Otto wanted the imperial title after his victories.
significance: It began the line of German emperors usually counted as the Holy Roman Empire.
place: Old St. Peter's Basilica, Rome, Vatican City

title: Hugh Capet is crowned king of the Franks
summary: Hugh Capet was crowned king of West Francia after the death of the last Carolingian king, Louis V.
reason: The great nobles and the archbishop of Reims chose Hugh over the Carolingian claimant Charles of Lorraine.
significance: His Capetian dynasty and its branches ruled France until the Revolution.

title: Astronomers record the supernova that made the Crab Nebula
summary: Chinese astronomers of the Song court recorded a guest star bright enough to be seen in daylight for weeks. It was the explosion that left the Crab Nebula.
reason: A massive star in the constellation Taurus ended its life in a supernova.
significance: Its records let modern astronomers date the Crab Nebula and its pulsar exactly.

title: Papal legates excommunicate the Patriarch of Constantinople
summary: Cardinal Humbert placed a bull excommunicating Patriarch Michael Cerularius on the altar of Hagia Sophia, and the patriarch answered by excommunicating the legates.
reason: Rome and Constantinople had long disagreed over papal authority, the Creed and church customs.
significance: It is the traditional date of the split between the Catholic and Orthodox churches.

title: William of Normandy wins the Battle of Hastings
summary: The Norman army of Duke William defeated the English under King Harold Godwinson, who was killed in the battle.
reason: William claimed the English throne after the death of Edward the Confessor and invaded when Harold was crowned.
significance: The Norman Conquest transformed England's rulers, language, law and ties to Europe.

title: Seljuks defeat the Byzantines at Manzikert
summary: The Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan defeated a Byzantine army and captured Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes near Manzikert in eastern Anatolia.
reason: Romanos marched east to stop Turkish raids into Byzantine Armenia and Anatolia.
significance: It opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement and led Byzantium to ask the West for help, a cause of the Crusades.

title: Pope Urban II calls for the First Crusade
summary: At the Council of Clermont, Pope Urban II urged Western Christians to march east to help Byzantium and free Jerusalem. The crowd answered with the cry Deus vult.
reason: Byzantine Emperor Alexios I had asked for soldiers against the Seljuks, and the pope also sought to assert papal leadership.
significance: It launched two centuries of crusading wars between Latin Christians and the Muslim world.

title: Crusaders capture Jerusalem
summary: Armies of the First Crusade broke into Jerusalem after a five-week siege and massacred much of its Muslim and Jewish population.
reason: Freeing the holy city was the goal of the crusade, and Fatimid Egypt had only recently retaken it from the Seljuks.
significance: It founded the Kingdom of Jerusalem and left a long memory of crusader violence in the region.

title: The Concordat of Worms ends the Investiture Controversy
summary: Emperor Henry V and Pope Callixtus II agreed that the Church would choose and invest bishops with their spiritual authority, while the emperor kept a role in granting their lands.
reason: For half a century popes and emperors had fought over who had the right to appoint bishops.
significance: It set an early boundary between church and state power in Europe.

title: Treaty of Zamora recognizes the Kingdom of Portugal
summary: Alfonso VII of Leon accepted Afonso Henriques as king of Portugal in a meeting at Zamora.
reason: Afonso Henriques had won battles against the Moors and against Leon and had already been calling himself king.
significance: It is taken as the founding date of Portugal as an independent kingdom.
participants: Alfonso VII of Leon and Castile

title: Abbot Suger consecrates the new choir of Saint-Denis
summary: The rebuilt choir of the abbey church of Saint-Denis, with pointed arches, ribbed vaults and large stained glass windows, was consecrated in the presence of King Louis VII.
reason: Abbot Suger wanted a church filled with light to honor God and the French monarchy, whose kings were buried there.
significance: It is considered the first Gothic building, the start of a style that spread across Europe.

title: Archbishop Thomas Becket is murdered in Canterbury
summary: Four knights of King Henry II killed Thomas Becket, Archbishop of Canterbury, inside his cathedral.
reason: Becket had resisted the king's attempts to control the Church, and the knights acted on Henry's angry words.
significance: Becket was quickly made a saint, and Henry had to do public penance and give way on church rights.

title: The Minamoto destroy the Taira at Dan-no-ura
summary: In a naval battle in the Shimonoseki Strait, the Minamoto fleet defeated the Taira clan. The child emperor Antoku drowned with many of the Taira.
reason: It was the final battle of the Genpei War between the two great warrior clans for control of Japan.
significance: Minamoto no Yoritomo went on to found the Kamakura shogunate and centuries of warrior rule.

title: Saladin crushes the crusaders at the Battle of Hattin
summary: Saladin's army surrounded and destroyed the army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem near the Horns of Hattin. King Guy of Lusignan was captured.
reason: Saladin had united Egypt and Syria and declared war after crusader attacks on Muslim caravans.
significance: The defeat left the crusader states almost defenceless and led to the fall of Jerusalem.
place: Horns of Hattin, near Tiberias, Israel

title: Saladin captures Jerusalem
summary: After a short siege, the defenders of Jerusalem under Balian of Ibelin surrendered the city to Saladin, who allowed most inhabitants to leave on payment of a ransom.
reason: The crusader army had been destroyed at Hattin, leaving the city with few soldiers.
significance: Its loss shocked Europe and provoked the Third Crusade.

title: Emperor Frederick Barbarossa drowns on crusade
summary: Holy Roman Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa drowned while crossing the Saleph River in Cilicia on his way to the Holy Land.
reason: He was leading a large German army in the Third Crusade to retake Jerusalem.
significance: Without him most of the German army broke up, weakening the crusade.

title: Death of Saladin in Damascus
summary: Saladin, sultan of Egypt and Syria and conqueror of Jerusalem, died of a fever in Damascus.
reason: He fell ill a few months after making peace with Richard the Lionheart.
significance: He was admired by Muslims and Christians alike, and his empire was divided among his heirs.

title: Fourth Crusade sacks Constantinople
summary: Crusaders and Venetians stormed Constantinople and plundered the city for three days, then set up a Latin Empire in its place.
reason: The crusaders were deep in debt to Venice and had been drawn into a Byzantine succession dispute that broke down into war.
significance: It shattered the Byzantine Empire and deepened the hostility between Catholic and Orthodox Christians.

title: Christian kingdoms defeat the Almohads at Las Navas de Tolosa
summary: The united armies of Castile, Aragon, Navarre and Portugal defeated the Almohad caliph Muhammad al-Nasir in the Sierra Morena.
reason: After the Christian defeat at Alarcos, Pope Innocent III backed a crusade and the Iberian kings joined forces.
significance: It broke Almohad power and opened southern Spain to the Christian reconquest.
wikipedia: Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa

title: Philip II of France wins the Battle of Bouvines
summary: King Philip II Augustus defeated the allied army of Emperor Otto IV, the Count of Flanders and English forces of King John near Bouvines.
reason: King John and his allies hoped to crush France and recover the English lands Philip had taken.
significance: It made France a leading power and helped force King John to accept Magna Carta.

title: King John agrees to Magna Carta at Runnymede
summary: Faced with rebel barons, King John of England set his seal to a charter of liberties at Runnymede beside the Thames.
reason: Heavy taxes, arbitrary rule and military failure in France had driven the barons to revolt.
significance: It became a lasting symbol of the principle that rulers are bound by law.

title: Fourth Lateran Council opens in Rome
summary: Pope Innocent III opened a great council of bishops in the Lateran Palace, which defined transubstantiation, required yearly confession and set rules for Jews and heretics.
reason: Innocent wanted to reform the Church, fight heresy and prepare a new crusade.
significance: Its decrees shaped Catholic practice for centuries.

title: Pope Honorius III approves the Dominican Order
summary: Pope Honorius III issued a bull confirming the Order of Preachers founded by Dominic de Guzman.
reason: Dominic wanted educated, poor preachers to counter heresy in southern France.
significance: The Dominicans became one of the most influential orders in teaching, theology and later the Inquisition.

title: Mongols defeat the Rus at the Kalka River
summary: A Mongol force under Jebe and Subutai routed a combined army of Rus princes and Cumans by the Kalka River.
reason: The Cumans asked the Rus for help against the Mongols, who were returning from a great raid around the Caspian.
significance: It was the first clash between the Mongols and the Rus, a warning of the conquest that followed.

title: Death of Francis of Assisi
summary: Francis of Assisi, founder of the Franciscan friars, died at the Porziuncola chapel near Assisi. He was made a saint less than two years later.
reason: His health had been broken by illness and his life of poverty.
significance: His order and his ideal of poverty and love of nature deeply shaped Christianity.

title: Mongols capture and destroy Kiev
summary: The Mongol army of Batu Khan stormed Kiev after a siege, killing most of its people and burning the city.
reason: The Mongols were conquering the Rus principalities as part of their great western campaign.
significance: It ended Kiev's role as the centre of the Rus, which came under the Golden Horde.

title: Mongols destroy the Hungarian army at Mohi
summary: The Mongols under Batu and Subutai crushed the army of King Bela IV of Hungary by the Sajo River. Much of Hungary was then ravaged.
reason: Hungary had sheltered the Cumans fleeing the Mongols and stood in the path of their invasion of Europe.
significance: It was the Mongols' greatest victory in Europe and devastated the kingdom of Hungary.
place: Muhi, near the Sajo River, Hungary

title: Death of the Great Khan Ogedei
summary: Ogedei, son of Genghis Khan and Great Khan of the Mongol Empire, died after a night of heavy drinking.
reason: He had long suffered from alcoholism.
significance: The news led the Mongol princes in Europe to turn back to settle the succession, sparing Western Europe.

title: Mongols capture Baghdad and end the Abbasid Caliphate
summary: Hulegu's Mongol army took Baghdad after a short siege. The city was sacked, the caliph al-Musta'sim was executed and a vast number of people were killed.
reason: The caliph had refused to submit to Hulegu, who was extending Mongol rule over the Middle East.
significance: It ended the Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad and is often seen as the end of the Islamic Golden Age.

title: Mamluks defeat the Mongols at Ain Jalut
summary: The Mamluk army of Egypt under Qutuz and Baybars defeated a Mongol force in the Jezreel Valley of Palestine.
reason: After taking Baghdad and Syria the Mongols threatened Egypt, but most of their army had withdrawn after the death of the Great Khan.
significance: It stopped the Mongol advance into the Middle East and Africa and made the Mamluks the leading Muslim power.

title: Nicaean forces retake Constantinople
summary: A small Nicaean force under Alexios Strategopoulos entered Constantinople while its Latin garrison was away, ending the Latin Empire.
reason: The Empire of Nicaea had been rebuilding Byzantine power in Anatolia and Greece since the sack of 1204.
significance: Michael VIII Palaiologos restored the Byzantine Empire, which lasted until 1453.

title: Simon de Montfort's Parliament meets
summary: Simon de Montfort, who held power after defeating Henry III, called a parliament in Westminster that included elected knights from the shires and burgesses from the towns.
reason: Montfort needed wide support for his government against the royalists.
significance: It is seen as a forerunner of the House of Commons and of representative government.

title: Kublai Khan proclaims the Yuan dynasty
summary: Kublai Khan adopted the Chinese dynastic name Great Yuan for his realm, ruling as a Chinese emperor from his new capital Dadu.
reason: Kublai wanted to present Mongol rule as a legitimate Chinese dynasty as he prepared to finish the conquest of the Song.
significance: The Yuan was the first foreign dynasty to rule all of China.

title: Death of Thomas Aquinas
summary: The Dominican theologian Thomas Aquinas died at the abbey of Fossanova while travelling to the Second Council of Lyon. His Summa Theologica was left unfinished.
reason: He fell ill on the journey, possibly after a head injury.
significance: His joining of Aristotle's philosophy with Christian theology became the basis of Catholic thought.

title: Yuan fleet destroys the last Song forces at Yamen
summary: The Yuan navy defeated the last fleet of the Southern Song off Yamen. The minister Lu Xiufu jumped into the sea with the boy emperor Zhao Bing.
reason: The Song court had fled south after the fall of its capital Lin'an, and Kublai's forces pursued it to the coast.
significance: It ended the Song dynasty and completed the Mongol conquest of China.

title: The Sicilian Vespers revolt against French rule
summary: At the hour of vespers on Easter Monday, the people of Palermo rose against the French soldiers of Charles of Anjou, and the revolt spread across Sicily.
reason: Sicilians resented heavy taxes and the harsh rule of the Angevin French.
significance: Sicily passed to the Crown of Aragon, starting a long war over southern Italy.

title: St. Lucia's flood drowns thousands in the Low Countries
summary: A storm surge on the North Sea broke through dunes and dikes in the Netherlands and northern Germany, killing tens of thousands of people.
reason: A powerful storm drove the sea over low lying land already weakened by earlier floods.
significance: It is one of the deadliest floods in history and greatly widened the Zuiderzee.

title: Tran Hung Dao defeats the Yuan fleet at Bach Dang
summary: Vietnamese forces led by Tran Hung Dao trapped the Yuan fleet on iron-tipped stakes driven into the bed of the Bach Dang River at low tide and destroyed it.
reason: Kublai Khan had sent a third invasion to conquer Dai Viet after earlier failures.
significance: It ended Mongol attempts to conquer Vietnam and made Tran Hung Dao a national hero.
place: Bach Dang River, Quang Ninh, Vietnam

title: Mamluks capture Acre, the last crusader stronghold
summary: The Mamluk army of Sultan al-Ashraf Khalil stormed Acre after a six-week siege. The remaining crusader towns on the coast were abandoned soon after.
reason: The Mamluks were driving the last Latin Christians from the Levant, and a massacre of Muslims in Acre gave them a pretext.
significance: It ended the crusader states in the Holy Land.

title: Flemish militias defeat French knights at Courtrai
summary: Flemish town militias, fighting on foot, routed a heavy French cavalry army outside Courtrai. Hundreds of gilded spurs taken from dead knights were hung in a local church.
reason: King Philip IV of France tried to absorb the County of Flanders, and the cloth towns rose against French rule and their pro-French patricians.
significance: It showed that disciplined infantry could beat mounted knights, a lesson repeated across the century.

title: French agents seize Pope Boniface VIII at Anagni
summary: Men sent by Philip IV of France and allied Roman nobles broke into the papal palace at Anagni and held Pope Boniface VIII captive for several days. The aged pope died weeks after his release.
reason: Philip and Boniface were locked in a struggle over the taxation of clergy and papal claims of supremacy over kings, set out in the bull Unam sanctam.
significance: The humiliation marked the decline of papal power over monarchs and opened the way to the Avignon papacy.

title: Scottish nobles sign the Declaration of Arbroath
summary: Scottish barons sent a letter to Pope John XXII asserting Scotland's independence and their right to choose their own king. It is dated at Arbroath Abbey.
reason: England refused to accept Robert the Bruce as king, and the pope had excommunicated him, so the Scots sought papal recognition.
significance: It became one of the most famous early statements of national sovereignty and of a king ruling by consent.
place: Arbroath Abbey, Arbroath, Scotland, United Kingdom

title: English longbowmen win the Battle of Crecy
summary: An English army under Edward III, dismounted and backed by massed longbows, destroyed a larger French army in northern France. Many French nobles died in repeated cavalry charges.
reason: Edward III claimed the French throne and was raiding through Normandy when Philip VI caught up with him.
significance: It was a turning point in the Hundred Years' War and in the decline of the mounted knight.

title: Emperor Charles IV issues the Golden Bull
summary: At the Imperial Diet in Nuremberg, Charles IV promulgated a decree fixing how the King of the Romans was elected by seven prince-electors and by majority vote.
reason: Disputed double elections had caused repeated civil wars in the Holy Roman Empire, and the electors wanted fixed rules free of papal interference.
significance: It served as the constitution of the Holy Roman Empire for over four centuries.

title: Black Prince captures King John II at Poitiers
summary: An outnumbered Anglo-Gascon army led by Edward the Black Prince defeated the French near Poitiers and captured King John II and his son.
reason: The Black Prince was leading a destructive raid through France, and John II intercepted him to end it.
significance: The king's capture threw France into crisis and led to the Treaty of Bretigny, which gave England large territories.

title: Zhu Yuanzhang proclaims the Ming dynasty
summary: The rebel leader Zhu Yuanzhang declared himself emperor in Nanjing, taking the reign name Hongwu and founding the Ming dynasty. His armies took the Yuan capital later that year.
reason: Famine, floods and the Red Turban rebellions had broken the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty, and Zhu had defeated his rival rebel warlords.
significance: It began nearly three centuries of Ming rule, one of the most stable and populous periods in Chinese history.

title: Muscovite army defeats the Golden Horde at Kulikovo
summary: Grand Prince Dmitry of Moscow led a coalition of Russian principalities to victory over the Tatar army of Mamai near the Don river.
reason: Moscow had grown strong enough to refuse tribute to the Golden Horde, and Mamai marched north to restore his authority.
significance: It was the first major Russian victory over the Horde and boosted Moscow as the leader of the Russian lands.

title: Portugal secures independence at Aljubarrota
summary: A Portuguese army under King John I and Nuno Alvares Pereira, aided by English archers, crushed a much larger Castilian invasion force.
reason: After the death of King Ferdinand I, John I of Castile claimed the Portuguese crown through his wife, and Portuguese supporters of the House of Aviz resisted.
significance: It secured Portuguese independence and the Aviz dynasty that later launched the age of exploration.

title: Serbs and Ottomans clash at the Battle of Kosovo
summary: A Serbian-led army under Prince Lazar fought the Ottoman army of Sultan Murad I on the Field of Blackbirds. Both rulers were killed and both armies suffered heavy losses.
reason: The Ottomans were expanding through the Balkans, and the Serbian principalities tried to halt them.
significance: Serbia soon became an Ottoman vassal, and the battle became a central event of Serbian national memory.

title: Timur defeats and captures Sultan Bayezid at Ankara
summary: The army of the Central Asian conqueror Timur routed the Ottoman army near Ankara and took Sultan Bayezid I prisoner.
reason: Timur and Bayezid were rival empire builders whose borders met in eastern Anatolia, and each sheltered the other's enemies.
significance: The defeat plunged the Ottoman state into a decade of civil war and delayed the fall of Constantinople by half a century.

title: Poland and Lithuania defeat the Teutonic Order
summary: A Polish and Lithuanian army under Wladyslaw II Jagiello and Vytautas defeated the Teutonic Knights at Grunwald. The Grand Master and much of the order's leadership were killed.
reason: The Teutonic Order and the Polish-Lithuanian union had long disputed Samogitia and other borderlands.
significance: It broke the power of the Teutonic Order and made Poland-Lithuania a leading power of Eastern Europe.

title: Jan Hus is burned at the stake in Constance
summary: The Czech reformer Jan Hus was condemned as a heretic by the Council of Constance and burned, despite a promise of safe conduct from Emperor Sigismund.
reason: Hus attacked clerical corruption and the sale of indulgences and questioned papal authority, which the council saw as a threat to church unity.
significance: His death sparked the Hussite movement in Bohemia and foreshadowed the Reformation.

title: Henry V wins the Battle of Agincourt
summary: A tired English army under Henry V, mostly archers, defeated a far larger French army on muddy ground in northern France.
reason: Henry V had revived the English claim to the French throne and invaded while France was divided by civil war.
significance: The victory let Henry conquer Normandy and become heir to the French crown by the Treaty of Troyes.

title: Joan of Arc is burned at the stake in Rouen
summary: Joan of Arc, the peasant girl who had led French armies to victory at Orleans, was burned in Rouen after a church trial controlled by the English.
reason: She was captured by Burgundian forces, sold to the English, and tried for heresy so that her victories and Charles VII's coronation would be discredited.
significance: She became a national symbol of France and was later declared a saint.

title: Ottomans crush a crusading army at Varna
summary: Sultan Murad II defeated a Hungarian and Polish crusader army near the Black Sea port of Varna. King Wladyslaw III of Poland and Hungary was killed in the battle.
reason: The crusade aimed to drive the Ottomans out of the Balkans and relieve Constantinople, breaking a recent peace treaty.
significance: It ended the last major European attempt to save Byzantium before the fall of Constantinople.

title: Oirat Mongols capture the Ming emperor at Tumu
summary: Oirat Mongol forces under Esen Taishi destroyed a large Ming army at the Tumu fortress and captured the Zhengtong Emperor.
reason: Trade disputes on the northern frontier led Esen to raid China, and the young emperor marched out on a poorly planned campaign urged by the eunuch Wang Zhen.
significance: The disaster turned Ming China toward a defensive frontier policy that led to the rebuilding of the Great Wall.

title: Constantinople falls to the Ottoman Turks
summary: After a siege of nearly two months, the army of Sultan Mehmed II stormed Constantinople. The last Byzantine emperor, Constantine XI, died in the fighting.
reason: The Ottomans had surrounded the shrunken Byzantine state for decades, and Mehmed II used giant cannon to breach its walls.
significance: It ended the Byzantine Empire and made the city the capital of the Ottoman Empire for nearly five centuries.

title: Henry Tudor defeats Richard III at Bosworth Field
summary: Henry Tudor's army defeated King Richard III in Leicestershire after key nobles changed sides. Richard was killed, the last English king to die in battle.
reason: Richard III had taken the throne in contested circumstances, and Lancastrian exiles backed Henry's claim.
significance: It ended the Wars of the Roses in practice and began the Tudor dynasty.
place: Bosworth Field, Leicestershire, England, United Kingdom

title: Spain orders the expulsion of its Jews
summary: Ferdinand and Isabella signed the Alhambra Decree, ordering all Jews in Castile and Aragon to convert to Christianity or leave by the end of July.
reason: The monarchs, urged by the Inquisition, wanted religious unity after the conquest of Granada and blamed Jews for influencing converts.
significance: It ended centuries of Jewish life in Spain and scattered Sephardic communities across the Mediterranean and beyond.

title: Columbus makes landfall in the Bahamas
summary: After crossing the Atlantic with three ships, Christopher Columbus landed on an island the Lucayan people called Guanahani and named it San Salvador.
reason: Columbus, sponsored by the Crown of Castile, sought a western sea route to Asia for trade in spices and gold.
significance: It began lasting contact between Europe and the Americas, with enormous consequences for both.

title: Spain and Portugal divide the world at Tordesillas
summary: Castile and Portugal agreed on a line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands: new lands west of it would go to Spain and lands east of it to Portugal.
reason: Columbus's voyage created a dispute over newly found lands, and both crowns wanted to avoid war.
significance: It shaped the colonial map, explaining why Brazil speaks Portuguese and most of Latin America Spanish.

title: Vasco da Gama reaches India by sea
summary: The Portuguese fleet of Vasco da Gama arrived near Calicut on the Malabar Coast after sailing around Africa, guided across the Indian Ocean by a local pilot.
reason: Portugal had spent decades exploring the African coast to reach the spice markets of Asia without Venetian and Muslim middlemen.
significance: Opening the sea route to India began European maritime empires in Asia and reshaped world trade.

title: Pedro Alvares Cabral reaches Brazil
summary: A Portuguese fleet bound for India under Pedro Alvares Cabral sighted land in South America, went ashore near Porto Seguro and claimed it for Portugal.
reason: Cabral swung far west into the Atlantic to catch favourable winds on the route around Africa.
significance: It began the Portuguese colonization of Brazil.

title: Michelangelo's David is unveiled in Florence
summary: Michelangelo's five-metre marble statue of the biblical David was unveiled outside the Palazzo Vecchio in Florence.
reason: The cathedral works had commissioned the statue, and the city chose a public site where it could stand for the defiant Florentine republic.
significance: It became the defining masterpiece of High Renaissance sculpture.

title: Portugal wins the naval Battle of Diu
summary: A Portuguese fleet under Francisco de Almeida defeated the combined fleets of the Mamluk Sultanate, the Gujarat Sultanate and the Zamorin of Calicut off Diu.
reason: Muslim and Indian powers, backed by Venice, wanted to break Portugal's attempt to control the spice trade of the Indian Ocean.
significance: It gave Portugal naval dominance in the Indian Ocean for most of the century.

title: Afonso de Albuquerque captures Goa
summary: Portuguese forces under Afonso de Albuquerque retook the island city of Goa from the Bijapur Sultanate after losing it earlier that year.
reason: Albuquerque wanted a permanent fortified base to control the sea lanes of western India.
significance: Goa became the capital of Portuguese India and stayed Portuguese until 1961.

title: Ottomans defeat the Safavids at Chaldiran
summary: Sultan Selim I's army, using artillery and firearms, defeated the cavalry of Shah Ismail I of Persia in northwestern Iran.
reason: The Sunni Ottomans feared the spread of Safavid Shia influence among the Turkmen tribes of Anatolia.
significance: It fixed the Ottoman-Persian frontier for generations and deepened the Sunni-Shia divide between the two empires.

title: Ottomans destroy the Mamluk army at Marj Dabiq
summary: Selim I defeated the Mamluk Sultan Qansuh al-Ghawri north of Aleppo. The sultan died on the field and Syria passed to the Ottomans.
reason: Rivalry over the frontier and fears of a Mamluk alliance with Safavid Persia drove Selim to attack.
significance: It opened the way to the Ottoman conquest of Egypt and made the Ottomans guardians of Mecca and Medina.

title: Martin Luther posts the Ninety-five Theses
summary: Martin Luther, a professor at Wittenberg, sent his Ninety-five Theses against the sale of indulgences to the Archbishop of Mainz and, by tradition, nailed them to the Castle Church door.
reason: Luther objected to the preaching of indulgences to raise money for St. Peter's Basilica and to the idea that forgiveness could be bought.
significance: It started the Protestant Reformation, which split Western Christianity.

title: Christian II carries out the Stockholm Bloodbath
summary: Days after being crowned King of Sweden, the Danish king Christian II had about eighty Swedish nobles, bishops and burghers executed in Stockholm's main square.
reason: Christian wanted to destroy the Swedish faction that opposed the Kalmar Union, using charges of heresy as cover.
significance: The massacre provoked the Swedish uprising led by Gustav Vasa that ended the union.

title: Magellan is killed at the Battle of Mactan
summary: Ferdinand Magellan and a small party of his crew were killed by warriors of the chief Lapulapu on Mactan island in the Philippines.
reason: Magellan had allied with the ruler of Cebu and tried to force Lapulapu to submit and convert.
significance: Lapulapu is remembered as the first Filipino hero to resist European rule, and the expedition went on without its leader.

title: Emperor Charles V outlaws Martin Luther
summary: After Luther refused to recant at the Diet of Worms, Charles V issued an edict declaring him an outlaw and banning his writings.
reason: Charles saw himself as the defender of the Catholic Church and wanted to stop the spread of Luther's ideas in the Empire.
significance: The edict could not be enforced, and Luther's protection by Saxony let the Reformation spread.

title: Tenochtitlan falls to Cortes and his allies
summary: After a long siege, Spanish forces under Hernan Cortes and tens of thousands of indigenous allies captured the Aztec capital and its last ruler, Cuauhtemoc.
reason: Cortes sought to conquer the Aztec Empire for Spain, and peoples such as the Tlaxcalans joined him against Aztec domination; smallpox had already ravaged the city.
significance: It ended the Aztec Empire and began three centuries of Spanish rule in Mexico.

title: The Victoria completes the first circumnavigation
summary: The ship Victoria, commanded by Juan Sebastian Elcano, reached Sanlucar de Barrameda with 18 survivors, three years after Magellan's fleet of five ships had set out.
reason: The expedition had sought a western route to the Spice Islands, and the survivors returned westward around Africa.
significance: It was the first voyage around the world and proved the true size of the Earth's oceans.

title: Gustav Vasa is elected King of Sweden
summary: The Swedish Riksdag, meeting at Strangnas, elected the rebel leader Gustav Eriksson Vasa as king.
reason: Gustav had led the uprising against Danish rule after the Stockholm Bloodbath.
significance: It ended the Kalmar Union and founded the independent Swedish state; 6 June is Sweden's national day.

title: Francis I is captured at the Battle of Pavia
summary: Imperial and Spanish troops of Charles V defeated the French army besieging Pavia and took King Francis I prisoner.
reason: France and the Habsburgs were fighting for control of the Duchy of Milan and northern Italy.
significance: It confirmed Habsburg dominance in Italy and showed the power of arquebus-armed infantry.

title: Babur wins the First Battle of Panipat
summary: Babur, a Timurid prince from Kabul, used field guns and mobile cavalry to defeat the much larger army of Ibrahim Lodi, Sultan of Delhi, who died in the battle.
reason: Babur sought a new kingdom in India, and discontented Lodi nobles invited him in.
significance: It founded the Mughal Empire, which ruled most of South Asia for two centuries.

title: Ottomans crush Hungary at the Battle of Mohacs
summary: Suleiman the Magnificent's army destroyed the Hungarian army in a single afternoon. King Louis II drowned while fleeing.
reason: The Ottomans were pushing up the Danube toward central Europe, and divided Hungary could raise only a small army.
significance: It ended the medieval Kingdom of Hungary, which was split between the Habsburgs and the Ottomans for 150 years.

title: Mutinous imperial troops sack Rome
summary: Unpaid soldiers of Charles V, including German Landsknechte, stormed Rome, killed thousands and looted the city while Pope Clement VII hid in Castel Sant'Angelo.
reason: Clement VII had joined the League of Cognac against Charles V, and the emperor's army in Italy had gone unpaid and out of control.
significance: It is often seen as the end of the High Renaissance in Rome and left the papacy under imperial influence.

title: The image of Our Lady of Guadalupe appears to Juan Diego
summary: According to tradition, the Virgin Mary appeared to the indigenous convert Juan Diego on the hill of Tepeyac, and her image was found imprinted on his cloak.
reason: The account arose in the decade after the Spanish conquest, when friars were seeking to convert the indigenous people of Mexico.
significance: Guadalupe became the most important religious and national symbol of Mexico and a major Catholic pilgrimage site.
place: Hill of Tepeyac, Mexico City, Mexico

title: Pizarro captures the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca
summary: Francisco Pizarro's small Spanish force ambushed the escort of the Inca ruler Atahualpa in the main square of Cajamarca, killed thousands and took him prisoner.
reason: Pizarro aimed to conquer the Inca Empire for its gold, and Atahualpa had just won a civil war against his brother Huascar.
significance: It began the Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire, the largest state in the Americas.

title: The Spanish execute the Inca emperor Atahualpa
summary: Although his subjects had filled a room with gold and silver as his ransom, Atahualpa was tried by the Spanish and executed by garrotte in Cajamarca.
reason: Pizarro feared Atahualpa would lead a rebellion and accused him of plotting and of killing his brother Huascar.
significance: His death left the Inca state leaderless and opened the road to Cusco for the conquerors.

title: Jacques Cartier claims Canada for France at Gaspe
summary: The French navigator Jacques Cartier planted a large cross on the shore of Gaspe Bay and claimed the land for King Francis I.
reason: Francis I sent Cartier to find a northwest passage to Asia and lands rich in gold.
significance: It marked the start of French claims in North America that grew into New France.

title: Francisco Pizarro founds Lima
summary: Pizarro founded the City of the Kings on the Rimac river near the Pacific coast as the capital of Spanish Peru.
reason: A coastal capital was easier to reach by sea from Panama and Spain than the Inca highland capital of Cusco.
significance: Lima became the seat of the Viceroyalty of Peru and the main city of Spanish South America.

title: Pope Paul III declares the indigenous peoples free
summary: In the bull Sublimis Deus, Pope Paul III declared that the native peoples of the Americas were rational beings who could not be enslaved or robbed of their property.
reason: Dominican friars in the Americas had reported the abuse and enslavement of indigenous people and appealed to Rome.
significance: It was an early papal statement of indigenous rights, though widely ignored in practice.

title: Pope Paul III approves the Society of Jesus
summary: With the bull Regimini militantis Ecclesiae, Paul III formally approved the religious order founded by Ignatius of Loyola and his companions.
reason: The church sought disciplined, educated priests to answer the Protestant challenge and to spread Catholicism overseas.
significance: The Jesuits became a leading force of the Counter-Reformation, of education and of missions in Asia and the Americas.

title: Charles V signs the New Laws for the Indies
summary: Charles V issued the New Laws in Barcelona, banning the enslavement of indigenous Americans and limiting the encomienda labour system.
reason: Reports by Bartolome de las Casas and others about the brutal treatment and collapse of native populations moved the crown to act.
significance: They were among the first laws of a colonial power meant to protect colonized people, though settler revolts forced their weakening.

title: The Council of Trent opens
summary: Bishops and theologians met in the city of Trent for the first session of an ecumenical council that would meet on and off until 1563.
reason: The Catholic Church needed to answer Protestant teachings and reform the abuses that had fuelled the Reformation.
significance: Its decrees defined Catholic doctrine and practice until the twentieth century and launched the Counter-Reformation.

title: Ivan IV is crowned the first Tsar of All Russia
summary: Grand Prince Ivan IV of Moscow was crowned in the Kremlin's Cathedral of the Dormition with the new title of Tsar.
reason: Moscow's rulers presented themselves as heirs of Byzantium and wanted a title equal to that of an emperor.
significance: It created the Tsardom of Russia, the autocratic state that lasted until 1917.
place: Cathedral of the Dormition, Moscow Kremlin, Russia

title: Francis Xavier brings Christianity to Japan
summary: The Jesuit missionary Francis Xavier landed at Kagoshima with the Japanese convert Anjiro and began the first Christian mission in Japan.
reason: Xavier had met Anjiro in Malacca and hoped Japan would be fertile ground for conversion.
significance: It began the Christian century in Japan, which saw hundreds of thousands of converts before persecution.

title: The Peace of Augsburg lets German princes choose their faith
summary: Charles V's brother Ferdinand and the princes of the Empire agreed that each ruler could choose Lutheranism or Catholicism for his territory.
reason: Decades of religious conflict and the Schmalkaldic War had shown that the Lutherans could not be suppressed by force.
significance: It brought sixty years of relative peace to Germany and fixed the principle that the ruler decides the religion.

title: The Shaanxi earthquake kills about 830,000 people
summary: A massive earthquake struck the Wei river valley in northern China. Many victims died when the cave dwellings cut into the soft loess hills collapsed.
reason: The quake came from movement on faults in the Weihe basin, and dense settlement in fragile loess caves multiplied the deaths.
significance: It is the deadliest earthquake on record.

title: The young Akbar becomes Mughal emperor
summary: Thirteen-year-old Akbar was enthroned on a brick platform in a garden at Kalanaur after the sudden death of his father Humayun.
reason: Humayun had died after a fall in his library, and the regent Bairam Khan moved quickly to secure the succession.
significance: Akbar became the greatest Mughal ruler, expanding the empire and promoting religious tolerance.

title: Mughals defeat Hemu at the Second Battle of Panipat
summary: Akbar's forces under Bairam Khan defeated the army of Hemu, who had seized Delhi, after Hemu was struck in the eye by an arrow.
reason: Hemu, a Hindu general of the Sur dynasty, had taken Delhi and Agra and claimed the throne after Humayun's death.
significance: It secured Mughal rule in northern India.

title: Elizabeth I is crowned Queen of England
summary: Elizabeth, daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn, was crowned in Westminster Abbey two months after the death of her half-sister Mary I.
reason: Mary I died without children, leaving the Protestant Elizabeth as heir under her father's will.
significance: Her 44-year reign settled the Church of England and saw England rise as a sea power.

title: Oda Nobunaga wins the Battle of Okehazama
summary: Oda Nobunaga's small force made a surprise attack during a rainstorm on the camp of the warlord Imagawa Yoshimoto, who was killed.
reason: Imagawa was marching on Kyoto with a large army and had invaded Nobunaga's province of Owari.
significance: The upset made Nobunaga a leading warlord and began the unification of Japan.

title: Spain founds St. Augustine in Florida
summary: Pedro Menendez de Aviles came ashore and founded the settlement of St. Augustine on the coast of Florida.
reason: Spain wanted to protect its treasure fleets and drive out French Huguenot settlers at nearby Fort Caroline.
significance: It is the oldest continuously inhabited European-founded city in the United States.

title: Poland and Lithuania form a commonwealth at Lublin
summary: The Sejm meeting in Lublin joined the Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania into one state with a common elected king and parliament.
reason: King Sigismund II Augustus had no heir, and Lithuania needed Polish support against Muscovy.
significance: It created the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, one of the largest states in Europe.

title: Miguel Lopez de Legazpi founds Spanish Manila
summary: Legazpi proclaimed the city of Manila on the site of a fortified Muslim settlement on Manila Bay and made it the capital of the Spanish Philippines.
reason: Spain wanted a base for trade with China and for its new colony in the islands.
significance: Manila became the Asian end of the galleon trade with Mexico, linking Asia and the Americas.

title: The Holy League defeats the Ottoman fleet at Lepanto
summary: A fleet of Spain, Venice, the Papal States and their allies under Don John of Austria destroyed most of the Ottoman navy at the mouth of the Gulf of Patras.
reason: The Ottomans had invaded Venetian Cyprus, and Pope Pius V formed a league to stop their naval expansion.
significance: It ended the image of Ottoman invincibility at sea and was the last great battle of oared galleys.
place: Gulf of Patras, off Lepanto (Nafpaktos), Greece

title: The St. Bartholomew's Day massacre begins in Paris
summary: Catholic mobs and royal troops killed the Huguenot leader Admiral Coligny and thousands of Protestants in Paris, and the killings spread to other French cities.
reason: Huguenot nobles had gathered for the wedding of Henry of Navarre and Margaret of Valois, and the court, led by Catherine de' Medici, feared a Protestant uprising.
significance: It reignited the French Wars of Religion and became a symbol of religious violence.

title: The last Inca ruler Tupac Amaru is executed in Cusco
summary: Tupac Amaru, ruler of the Neo-Inca State of Vilcabamba, was captured by Spanish forces and beheaded in the main square of Cusco.
reason: Viceroy Francisco de Toledo was determined to end the independent Inca state in the mountains.
significance: It ended the last independent Inca state.

title: Tycho Brahe observes a new star in Cassiopeia
summary: The Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe noticed a bright new star in the constellation Cassiopeia and measured that it showed no parallax, so it lay far beyond the Moon.
reason: The star was a supernova, and Tycho's careful measurements tested the belief that the heavens never change.
significance: It undermined the Aristotelian idea of unchanging heavens and made Tycho's name in astronomy.

title: The Warsaw Confederation guarantees religious freedom
summary: Nobles of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth signed an act promising peace among people of different faiths and barring persecution for religion.
reason: After the death of the last Jagiellonian king, the nobility, divided among Catholics, Protestants and Orthodox, wanted to prevent religious war during the royal election.
significance: It was one of the first legal guarantees of religious tolerance in Europe.

title: Oda and Tokugawa gunners win the Battle of Nagashino
summary: Massed arquebusiers of Oda Nobunaga and Tokugawa Ieyasu, firing from behind wooden palisades, destroyed the cavalry charges of Takeda Katsuyori.
reason: Takeda Katsuyori had besieged Nagashino castle, and Nobunaga and Ieyasu marched to relieve it.
significance: It broke the Takeda clan and showed the decisive power of firearms in Japanese warfare.

title: King Sebastian of Portugal dies at Alcacer Quibir
summary: A Portuguese crusading army was annihilated by the Moroccan Saadi army near Ksar el-Kebir. Three kings died, including the young Sebastian of Portugal.
reason: Sebastian backed a deposed Moroccan sultan, Abu Abdallah, against his uncle Abd al-Malik in hope of a North African crusade.
significance: Sebastian died without heir, which led to Spain taking the Portuguese crown in 1580, while Morocco gained new prestige.

title: Northern Dutch provinces sign the Union of Utrecht
summary: Holland, Zeeland, Utrecht and other northern provinces of the Habsburg Netherlands agreed to act together in defence and foreign policy against Spain.
reason: The revolt against Philip II's taxes and religious persecution needed a firm alliance after the southern provinces moved toward reconciliation with Spain.
significance: It became the founding document of the Dutch Republic.

title: Juan de Garay refounds Buenos Aires
summary: Juan de Garay, leading settlers from Asuncion, founded a permanent city on the Rio de la Plata on the site of an earlier abandoned settlement.
reason: Spain wanted a port on the Atlantic to link Paraguay and the Andes with Spain by sea.
significance: Buenos Aires grew into the capital of Argentina and one of the largest cities in the Americas.

title: Pope Gregory XIII issues the calendar reform bull
summary: With the bull Inter gravissimas, Gregory XIII ordered that ten days be dropped in October 1582 and introduced new leap year rules, creating the Gregorian calendar.
reason: The Julian calendar had drifted about ten days from the solar year, moving the date of Easter away from the spring equinox.
significance: The Gregorian calendar became the civil calendar of nearly the whole world.

title: Oda Nobunaga dies in the Honnoji Incident
summary: The general Akechi Mitsuhide turned on his lord Oda Nobunaga and attacked him at the Honnoji temple in Kyoto, where Nobunaga took his own life.
reason: Mitsuhide's motives remain debated: personal grievances, ambition and fear for his position have all been suggested.
